Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
I try to erase the memory of the event
I think about why the event has happened to me

Threat.value: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
Being superalert or watchful or on guard

Memory.value: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order
I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

issues.item: Triggers: Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
issues.explanation: For chronic physical abuse by a romantic partner, being triggered by male presence and related people is coherent, but explosion/bang sounds points toward combat, accidents, or blast-related trauma and is hard to reconcile as a core trigger here without any matching assault-context cue elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: The rest of the profile reflects fear, avoidance, hypervigilance, fragmented memory, and negative self/world appraisals. Endorsing risky behavior pulls in the opposite direction and is not supported by other selected items; it reads as a different coping/symptom pattern than the otherwise strongly avoidant-threat profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Lost Community: I have lost my connection to my community and culture
issues.explanation: A marked loss of connection to community and culture is not well anchored to the rest of this intimate-partner-violence profile. The other appraisals center on danger, contamination, and shattered beliefs, but nothing else suggests cultural/community rupture, making this item feel clinically disconnected rather than tightly linked to the stated trauma formulation.

vignette:
Margaret, an 80-year-old European American woman who had worked for decades as a social worker, came to treatment after years of living with the aftereffects of a violent relationship that she still described with a kind of stunned disbelief. When she was younger, she had been involved with a man she trusted at first, a man who became physically abusive in private and whose temper seemed to erupt without warning. She could still picture it in fractured pieces: the hallway, a hand gripping her arm, a door slamming hard enough to make her jump, the awful sense of being trapped alone with him. Even now, she said, the memory would not settle into a proper sequence; it came back as a few stark moments, each one like a photograph she could not arrange into a whole story. Looking back, what overwhelmed her most was grief, not only for what she had endured but for the person she had been before it happened.

In the years that followed, certain moments and places became charged with danger for her. If she found herself alone with a man, if a relative or other known man entered the room, or if she heard a door open or slam, her body reacted before she could think. The sound of a door in her apartment building or at the grocery store could jolt her into the past, and the sight of a man standing too close could make her stomach tighten and send her scanning for the nearest exit. Those triggers seemed to pull the old fragments of memory into the present, and with them came the conviction that the world had changed beyond repair. She had come to believe that people could not be trusted, that the assumptions she once lived by had been destroyed, and that what happened to her had left her somehow dirty, contaminated, and set apart from other people. The more she remembered, the more she felt those beliefs harden. The more she felt trapped by the image of that frightened woman in the past, the more any man, any familiar face linked to family or acquaintanceship, or any sudden sound of a door could seem ominous and personally aimed at her.

Margaret tried to manage this in ways that made sense to her at the time. She began avoiding the parts of the day and the situations she knew might bring nightmares, staying busy late into the evening or going to bed at odd hours in an effort to outrun them. She also tried to erase the memory from her mind, pushing away the scenes that arrived in those picture-like flashes, though the harder she tried, the more they seemed to press back. She spent long stretches thinking about why the event had happened to her, searching for some explanation that might restore order, but the questions only seemed to deepen her sense that the world was fundamentally unsafe and that she could not trust anyone not to harm her. Her efforts to blank out the past and make sense of it also kept the memories near the surface; whenever they surfaced, they brought fresh waves of mistrust and shame, and those beliefs in turn made her more likely to avoid sleep, social contact, and any setting where men might be present.

By the time she sought help, her daily life had narrowed considerably. As a retired social worker, Margaret still lived independently, but even ordinary routines had become organized around vigilance. She entered buildings with her eyes on the exits, noting who was nearby and where she might move quickly if she needed to leave. She described herself as superalert and watchful, never fully settling, and her sleep was broken by difficulty falling asleep and by waking in the night. The nights felt especially precarious because she feared the dreams that seemed to gather in certain hours, and the lack of sleep made her even more on guard the next day. That constant state of alertness also made her more susceptible to seeing danger in the presence of men or hearing a door as a warning, and each new alarm pushed her back toward avoiding people, erasing memories, or trying again to figure out why it had happened. In her mind, those attempts were necessary protections, yet they also kept confirming that the world was unsafe, that she remained contaminated by what was done to her, and that her life was still organized around the original violence.

She finally came for treatment because she was exhausted by the cycle and frightened by how much smaller her world had become. What she most wanted was to sleep without dread and to feel less haunted by the certainty that she could never fully trust another person again.
